summary:
### TL;DR
- **Copilot server-to-server authentication (public preview):** GitHub Apps installed on an organization can now call Copilot through the Copilot SDK using short-lived installation tokens instead of a signed-in user's credentials. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-27-github-copilot-supports-server-to-server-authentication))
- **Dependabot alert assignment needs a license:** The docs now state that assigning Dependabot alerts requires a GHAS or Code Security license, including on public repositories. ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts))
- Neither item directly changes GitHub Actions behavior.

### Action required
Nothing this time.

If your public repositories assign Dependabot alerts without a GHAS or Code Security license, check whether the clarified requirement affects that workflow. No deadline is stated. ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts))

### Security improvements
- **Workload-owned identity for Copilot automation (public preview).** Agents and services built with the Copilot SDK can act on behalf of an organization without relying on a signed-in user's credentials. ([changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-10-27-github-copilot-supports-server-to-server-authentication))
  - **How it works:** Give a GitHub App the read-only **Copilot Requests** organization permission, install it on the org, and pass a short-lived installation access token to the SDK.
  - **Governance:** Usage is attributed and billed to the owning organization. The org's model policies, budgets, and spending controls apply.
  - **Oversight:**
    - Org owners can review which apps have access.
    - App-attributed usage shows up in AI usage CSV reports via the `app_client_id` field.
    - Owners can revoke access by suspending or uninstalling the app.
  - **Why it matters:** This is a way to move Copilot automations off personal tokens tied to individual users and onto short-lived, org-scoped app credentials.

### Docs changes worth reading
- **Dependabot alerts: alert ownership and assignments.** A sentence was added stating that assigning Dependabot alerts requires a GHAS or Code Security license, including for public repositories. Previously the page only said users with write access or higher could assign alerts to collaborators, teams, or AI agents. ([page](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts), [commit](https://github.com/github/docs/commit/7fe47178072c0873f7fd273be488932de091ad55))

changelog.title: GitHub Copilot supports server-to-server authentication
changelog.text: GitHub Copilot now supports server-to-server authentication for GitHub Apps installed on organizations, available in public preview. Services and agents built with the GitHub Copilot SDK can now make requests on behalf of an organization without relying on a signed-in user’s credentials. This workload-owned identity helps agents and automated services operate reliably at larger scale without tying their authentication or usage to individual users. Developers can give a GitHub App the read-only Copilot Requests organization permission, install the app on an organization, and pass a short-lived installation access token to the Copilot SDK. Usage is attributed and billed to the organization that owns the installation. The organization’s model policies, budgets, and spending controls apply. Organization owners can review which apps have access, identify app-attributed usage in AI usage CSV reports using the app_client_id field, and stop an app’s access by suspending or uninstalling it. To get started, see server-to-server authentication for the GitHub Copilot SDK and managing GitHub App access to your organization’s Copilot . The post GitHub Copilot supports server-to-server authentication appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
